titre: Beethoven's Hair: A Woman's Lock, Then the Lead
accroche: The lead theory about Beethoven rested on a lock of hair that was not his. Two authenticated locks nonetheless contain a lot of it
contenu_vulgarise:
Tradition has it that after Beethoven's death in 1827, the young musician Ferdinand Hiller, fifteen, cut a lock of hair from him. Analyses of this lock argued for lead poisoning. In 2023, a genome sequencing showed that it was not Beethoven's.

## A woman's lock

In 1802, Beethoven asks that his illness be described and made public after his death. Biographers have since proposed diagnoses in great numbers. The team of Tristan Begg, Johannes Krause, and their colleagues therefore attempts a genomic analysis, adapting ancient-DNA methods to very small hair samples. It examines eight locks attributed to Beethoven, of independent provenance. Five come from the same man of European origin: the authors judge them almost certainly authentic. At least two do not come from Beethoven. Hiller's comes from a woman.

Yet the earlier analyses that argued for lead poisoning were carried out on this lock. According to the Beethoven-Haus press release, these results no longer hold for Beethoven, and future measurements of lead, opiates, or mercury will have to be carried out on authenticated samples. The shift is methodological: before measuring anything, one must prove whose hair it is.

## What the DNA says about his illnesses

The genome, sequenced at 24-fold coverage, offers no genetic explanation for the hearing loss or the digestive troubles. It reveals a predisposition to liver disease and an infection with the hepatitis B virus for at least the months before his death. Alcohol, whose real extent remains unknown, is added as a plausible cause of the liver disease that killed him.

## The lead, all the same

In 2024, Nader Rifai, Paul Jannetto, and their colleagues measure the metals in two of the authenticated locks, those known as the Bermann and Halm-Thayer locks. The lead reaches 258 and 380 micrograms per gram of hair, against a reference interval below 4. For the Halm-Thayer lock, a conversion formula gives an estimated blood lead level of 69 to 71 micrograms per deciliter. The authors write that these levels do not support the idea that lead caused Beethoven's death, and that it may have contributed to the digestive, kidney, and hearing problems he suffered from.

The lead theory therefore rested on a wrong sample, and yet high levels were measured on the right ones. As for the death itself, hepatitis B, the fragile liver, and alcohol offer a plausible explanation, according to the 2023 authors.

None of these analyses establishes what made Beethoven deaf: lead is put forward only as a possible contributor, and the genome finds no cause there.

repere.texte: Halm-Thayer lock: 380 micrograms of lead per gram of hair (369 by the second method); Bermann lock: 258 (254). Reference interval: less than 4.
repere.source: Rifai et al., “High Lead Levels in 2 Independent and Authenticated Locks of Beethoven's Hair,” Clinical Chemistry 70(6), 2024, p. 878

carte.punch: Beethoven's lead: a woman's lock, then two heavily loaded authenticated locks.
carte.idee: In 2023, the DNA of eight locks attributed to Beethoven shows that Hiller's, already analyzed for lead, comes from a woman. In 2024, two authenticated locks nonetheless show 258 and 380 micrograms of lead per gram, without that explaining his death.

quiz.question: Why don't the 2024 lead measurements prove that lead killed Beethoven?
choix: Because the two locks measured had not been authenticated
Because lead was absent from both locks, contrary to what was believed
Because the 2023 genome had already established mercury poisoning
Because the authors judge these levels insufficient to cause death on their own
quiz.explication: Both locks, Bermann and Halm-Thayer, had been authenticated in 2023, and the lead in them is very high. But the authors write that these levels do not support the idea that it caused his death, and that it may have contributed to digestive, kidney, and hearing problems. The genome did not establish mercury poisoning.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 2023 sequencing, whom did the lock cut by Ferdinand Hiller, the one used for the first lead analyses, belong to?
choix: Beethoven, but taken by mistake after Hiller's
One of the five men whose locks were judged authentic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The genome shows that this lock comes from a woman, which voids the old lead measurements made on it in Beethoven's name.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2023 genome reveal about Beethoven's illnesses?
choix: A mutation responsible for his progressive deafness
A genetic lead poisoning passed down from his mother
A liver predisposition and a hepatitis B infection
A complete absence of any predisposition or infection
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The genome finds no genetic cause for the deafness or the digestive troubles, but reveals a predisposition to a fragile liver and an infection with hepatitis B.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Beethoven ask for in 1802, in the Heiligenstadt Testament?
choix: That his hair be analyzed by future science
That his illness be described and made public after his death
That his body never be autopsied
That his biographers keep his health problems permanently silent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Heiligenstadt Testament, dated October 6, 1802, explicitly asks that Beethoven's illness be described and known after his death.
